title: Sodium Molybdate
description: Anodic corrosion inhibitor for cooling water treatment systems.

details.longDescription:
Sodium molybdate dihydrate (Na2MoO4·2H2O, CAS 10102-40-6) is a white crystalline powder supplied by Global Chemicals LLC at 99% purity in 25 kg bags and drums from stock in Muscat, as the chromate-free anodic corrosion inhibitor for closed cooling and chilled-water systems, used on its own or together with nitrite. It has low acute toxicity and is not classified as dangerous goods for transport, but it is an industrial water-treatment chemical for closed, non-potable circuits: it is not a drinking-water treatment and must not be dosed into potable water or into water that contacts food or product.

How it protects. In the presence of dissolved oxygen, molybdate adsorbs on steel at the anodic sites and forms a thin, insoluble ferric molybdate film that stops iron dissolving. Typical treatment holds 100–500 mg/L of molybdate as MoO4 in closed loops, at pH 8.0–10.0, often blended with nitrite, azoles for copper and silicate or phosphonate for mixed metals; the molybdate residual is easy to test in the field, which makes dosing control simple. Because it is anodic, under-dosing gives localised pitting rather than protection, so residuals are checked and topped up rather than assumed, and losses to leaks and make-up water are replaced. In open cooling towers it is used at low levels in phosphate-free programmes where phosphate discharge is restricted, subject to any local limit on molybdenum itself.

Where it is used in Oman: chilled-water loops of district cooling, hotels, malls and hospitals; closed process-cooling circuits in factories and power plants; heating and hot-water loops; hydrostatic test and lay-up water for new pipelines and vessels; closed utility cooling circuits in food, beverage and pharmaceutical plants, with no contact with product or potable water; and engine and heat-transfer coolants. It is also a molybdenum micronutrient for legumes and some vegetables in fertiliser blends, and a reagent in laboratory phosphate analysis.

Handling and storage: sodium molybdate has low acute toxicity and most suppliers do not classify it as hazardous under GHS, although some safety data sheets list irritation, so follow the SDS supplied with the lot; avoid dust and ingestion, wear gloves and safety glasses, and keep bags closed and dry. Molybdenum is regulated in some wastewater discharges, so check local limits before draining treated loop water. Every lot carries a certificate of analysis giving assay and molybdenum content, and a safety data sheet; our water-treatment team supplies test kits and dosing calculations for closed systems.

Delivery is same day within Muscat, next day to Sohar, two to three days to Salalah and Duqm, and by road across the GCC with a certificate of origin. Request a quote with the quantity and system volume.

faqs.question: What is an oxygen scavenger and why is it needed in boiler water treatment?
faqs.answer: An oxygen scavenger is a chemical that reacts with dissolved oxygen in water, converting it to non-corrosive compounds before it can attack metal surfaces. In boiler systems, even trace amounts of dissolved oxygen (0.007 mg/L is the target for high-pressure boilers) cause pitting corrosion — small, deep pits that rapidly penetrate boiler tubes and cause catastrophic failure. Mechanical deaeration (deaerators, vacuum degassers) removes most oxygen, but chemical oxygen scavengers are used as a final polishing step. Common oxygen scavengers used in Oman boiler water treatment include catalysed sodium sulphite (for low-pressure boilers below 40 bar), DEHA (diethylhydroxylamine, for medium and high-pressure boilers), and hydrazine alternatives (carbohydrazide, methylethylketoxime) for power station and high-pressure applications.

faqs.question: What is the correct oxygen scavenger dosage for boiler water treatment?
faqs.answer: Oxygen scavenger dosage depends on the dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration in the boiler feedwater after deaeration and the specific product's stoichiometry. As a general rule: sodium sulphite reacts at approximately 8 mg of sodium sulphite per mg of dissolved oxygen (stoichiometric). To maintain a protective residual of 10–30 mg/L excess sodium sulphite in the feedwater, total dosing must account for both reaction with incoming DO and maintaining this residual. For DEHA and organic scavengers, typical dose rates are 0.2–0.5 mg/L in feedwater. Always test DO and residual scavenger concentration weekly — follow the boiler manufacturer's water-quality guidelines and your treatment programme specification to stay within warranty.

faqs.question: What type of oxygen scavenger should I use in Oman's industrial boiler systems?
faqs.answer: The correct oxygen scavenger type depends on boiler operating pressure and temperature. For low-pressure steam boilers (below 40 bar) in Oman's industrial facilities — common in food processing, hospitals, and laundries — catalysed sodium sulphite is the standard choice: low cost, reliable, and compatible with most treatment programmes. For medium-pressure boilers (40–100 bar) in industrial process plants and power generation, DEHA (diethylhydroxylamine) is preferred because it does not add sulphate or dissolved solids to the boiler water and is volatile, so it also protects the condensate system. For high-pressure power station boilers (above 100 bar), low-solids organic scavengers such as carbohydrazide or erythorbic acid are used to avoid total dissolved solids (TDS) buildup. Global Chemicals LLC supplies all three types for Oman's industrial boiler market.

faqs.question: Can oxygen scavengers be used in closed cooling loop systems?
faqs.answer: Yes. Oxygen scavengers are used in closed cooling water loops to eliminate the oxygen that causes pitting corrosion in pipework, heat exchangers, and chiller circuits. For closed systems — unlike open cooling towers where oxidising biocides are also needed — the primary corrosion mechanism is dissolved oxygen, not scale or biological fouling. After initial system fill and commissioning, a one-time or periodic dose of oxygen scavenger (typically sodium sulphite at 20–50 mg/L residual) along with a film-forming corrosion inhibitor provides effective long-term protection. Closed system oxygen scavenger treatment is particularly important in Oman's chilled water systems where steel pipework is common and the cost of corrosion leak repairs is high.
